newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: ALCOHOL FIRMS SEEK ADVERTISING FREEDOM IN E.EUROPE.
newsitem.headline: ALCOHOL FIRMS SEEK ADVERTISING FREEDOM IN E.EUROPE.

text.p: Western manufacturers of alcoholic beverages urged Eastern European countries on Wednesday against creating state legislation to regulate alcohol advertising.

Richard Owen, a top representative of companies that produce and market alcoholic drinks in Europe, told an advertising conference in Prague that self-regulation was cheaper and worked better than state control.

"We believe that self-regulation has many advantages over a purely regulatory approach," Richard Owen, chairman of the Amsterdam Group Working Committee, told the "West Goes East" conference on advertising and self-regulation.
"Experience shows that it is usually quicker, more flexible and cheaper for the consumer," he said.
Most of Western Europe has a self-regulatory advertising framework, but several countries have strict limits on advertising alcoholic beverages.
A law in France called the "Loi Sapin" basically bans tobacco and alcohol advertising.
In Britain a drinks industry body called the Portman Group is meant to promote sensible drinking and ensure, among other things, that alcohol advertising is not targeted at under-age drinkers.
But the group has come under recent pressure over marketing for fruit-flavoured alcoholic drinks -- so-called "alcopops" -- from critics who say it is wrongly aimed at young people.

Manufacturers of alcoholic beverages and a wide range of other consumer products, who face crowded markets in the West, have rushed into Eastern Europe in recent years and hope to avoid strict controls on advertising.
The Amsterdam Group, an association of 15 companies that produce and market alcoholic beverages in Europe, says its goals include strengthening political and social acceptance of alcoholic beverages.
It also says it is important to recognise and combat alcohol misuse.
Owen said governments could play a valuable role in regulating the advertisement of alcohol, but should leave most of the regulatory process to the industry.
The ideal solution, he said, appeared to be a minimum framework of legislation within which self-regulation could operate speedily and effectively.
A purely legislative approach could be rigid and time-consuming to enforce.
"But self-regulation is not, or must not be, a soft option or merely a public relations exercise," he said. REUTER
